Indexed Annuities Boost Private Credit
 
Plus, China’s social-media shoppers and one Fed official’s worries
 
 
TRAVIS DOVE/BLOOMBERG NEWS
 

Some economic shocks look like bumps in the road—tariffs, to which businesses adjust, or a war with Iran that raises oil prices temporarily. But economists increasingly believe that higher U.S. interest rates will define the rest of the decade.

 

So concludes The Wall Street Journal’s latest survey of forecasters. The surveyed analysts don’t see the recent surge in long-term yields to quarter-century highs as a temporary blip that will fade as inflation cools. Instead, they expect higher long-term yields to be sustained.

 

Treasurys set the tempo for borrowing costs across the economy. Higher yields mean higher mortgage rates and more expensive borrowing for companies. They also increase the burden on the federal budget, where interest on the national debt now exceeds military spending.

 

Below, some of the best analysis and insight from WSJ writers and columnists, the Dow Jones Newswires team and occasionally beyond, on investing, the wealth-management business and more.

Market Talk

 

From Dow Jones Newswires

 

Amid speculation of a Mattel sale, investors are taking a closer look at toy stocks and realizing that there is underappreciated value, Seaport analysts say in a research note. “We think investors are in the process of rediscovering the toy industry’s stability, recession-resistance, and strong free cash flow generation,” the analysts write. “We think all toy stocks, including Mattel, will experience multiple expansion as a result.” Seaport upgrades Mattel to buy from neutral and says its upgrade isn’t contingent upon an acquisition, which has been subject to takeover speculation many times in the past. “Based on our conversations with key players in the toy industry over the weekend, though, it seems more likely this time,” the analysts say. “While we’ve been critical of Mattel’s performance, we do think there is plenty of value if managed properly.” (connor.hart@wsj.com)

 

The European Union’s agreement with China to curb its exports of hybrid cars into the region could be a blueprint for future deals, Capital Economics says in a note Monday. “There is mounting pressure from other industries such as chemicals and machine tools for similar for protection,” it says. The EU said it will cap hybrid and plug-in hybrid car imports from China at 350,000 units annually for four years. “If extended to all the industries that are targeted by the EU ‘s Industrial Accelerator Act this could potentially affect around a quarter of all imports, which would have a bigger impact on the wider economy,” Capital Economics says, adding that it remains to be seen whether China will agree to similar restrictions on other and potentially much larger sectors. (edith.hancock@wsj.com)
